scope: Persona audit of actual month-one-v5, not observed audience data

episodes.current_title: First gym visit—what do you do first?
episodes.current_action: Ask the gym about an orientation. Put the routine in your phone so you can follow it there.
episodes.strength: a very relevant first decision; practical orientation request; acknowledgment that a video cannot check setup.
episodes.gap: “bring a beginner routine” sends me to solve a large missing prerequisite. The action frame still displays category names rather than a completed first-visit note. This is an incomplete handoff, not a missing action.
episodes.proposed_hook: “First gym visit? Don't arrive with only a membership.”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show a phone note containing my planned visit, a saved routine link and the exact orientation question: “Can someone show me how to set up the equipment in this routine?” End on “Save your plan and ask about an orientation before you go.” A real, checked start-here resource must exist before the clip points to it.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: the note and question are editorial examples. Selecting/recommending an actual program needs current source, suitability and scope review. Do not disguise a generic short as individualized instruction.

episodes.current_title: Machines can be a valid place to start.
episodes.current_action: Ask for the setup, choose an option in your routine, and record its settings.
episodes.strength: the belonging line—“You do not have to earn your place at the gym with a barbell”—and the useful advice to save machine settings.
episodes.gap: this contains one of the month's strongest experienced-person tips, but the diagram only shows machine versus free weight. I do not see what “save the settings” means.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Think machines don't count? You can start there.”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show a sample note with fields for exact machine, seat/back-pad setting, load, reps and setup notes. Display a fictional illustrative entry only if numbers cannot be mistaken for a recommendation; blanks with a filled machine name are sufficient. End on “After someone checks your setup, save the settings.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain E06's equipment-specific skill and non-interchangeability limits. Do not imply identical displayed loads across machines or a universal safety ranking.

episodes.current_title: Are you rushing your next set?
episodes.current_action: Follow your routine, use a timer, and note whether performance drops across sets.
episodes.strength: rest is part of the session; a timer is an observable action; the current trial qualification is honest.
episodes.gap: the prominent 1:00 versus 3:00 visual may be what I remember even though narration says no universal rule. The answer I need is how to apply my plan, not mainly which trial was conducted.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Starting the next set just because you feel awkward waiting?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: a routine's rest instruction becomes a matching timer; the log records what happened in the next set. Use a placeholder or explicitly illustrative instruction unless a particular plan is actually being demonstrated. End on “Use your routine's rest guidance and record the next set.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain E16's small trained-men sample and limited comparison. Do not introduce a universal rest dose. This episode has a prepared citation experiment: changing its hook, scene or timing requires versioning and rebuilding both matched conditions; do not silently replace only one.

episodes.current_title: A short walk can fit into your real week.
episodes.current_action: Choose a time and route that fit your current ability.
episodes.strength: already strong lifestyle integration: after lunch, familiar route, indoor backup. It already contains a simple cue and contingency; no mental-model lecture is needed.
episodes.gap: the line and two dots are a route symbol, not a recognizable daily situation. The opening is agreeable but low in tension.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Your calendar is full. Where does a walk fit?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show a lunch break turning into a calendar note with a suitable route and a weather/access alternative. End on “Choose your next walking window and one backup.” D could close his laptop and head outside rather than stand under a diagram.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain BPF01's adult scope and distinction between a starting action and full activity guidance. Do not promise a particular body outcome or universal duration. Preserve/version the existing motion experiment if changing the implementation.

episodes.current_title: What weight should you start with?
episodes.current_action: Record the load and how the set went. Progress using your routine, with control.
episodes.strength: the direct question is strong. Individual setup and a manageable learning load are sensible boundaries.
episodes.gap: the hook promises a selection method; most of the answer delegates to an instructor. That can feel evasive if I cannot identify whom to ask. “Progress using your routine” also assumes I understand progression. The adult audience is briefly displaced by a spoken 16–17-year-old qualification.
episodes.proposed_hook: retain “What weight should you start with?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: demonstrate the exact help request: “Can you check this setup and help me find a starting load for this routine?” Show where that load and the person's observation are recorded. A subsequent researched explainer should translate the routine's progression instructions; do not cram that into this clip.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: a new self-selection method, load range, rep target or progression rule needs adult-specific evidence and qualified review. F02 is youth guidance and should not be the only visible authority for a primarily adult load-selection clip. State adult scope clearly; retain under-18 guidance where relevant without making the main lesson switch populations midstream.

episodes.current_title: Soreness is not your progress score.
episodes.current_action: Keep a simple training log instead of rating the workout by tomorrow’s ache.
episodes.strength: the existing unscheduled hook “Not sore—did the workout count?” meets the viewer at a recognizable doubt. Retain the distinction between soreness and sharp/worsening pain.
episodes.gap: “keep a log” has recurred but the month has not actually taught me to make one. The current ticks suggest tracking, without demonstrating a record.
episodes.proposed_hook: promote the existing alternative: “Not sore—did the workout count?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show one session entry with exercise, load, reps and a note; then show the same exercise in a later session. End on “Record what you completed today.” Do not use invented improvements as if they were observed results.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: preserve F08/E13 limits. Neither a completed log nor rising numbers alone proves muscle growth; no soreness is not a reason to dismiss a session.

episodes.current_title: First run club: what should you check?
episodes.current_action: Check the event details and ask who supports the slowest group.
episodes.strength: one of the strongest specific checklists in the month; addresses a real practical mismatch hidden by “all paces.”
episodes.gap: the message I would send is more useful than another list of categories. Existing BPK02 already supplies the deeper checklist, but the connection is weak.
episodes.proposed_hook: “The run club says ‘all paces.’ Will they actually wait for you?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show the draft: “I'm new. Which distance and pace group would suit a beginner, are walk breaks welcome, and who stays with the last group?” End with “Check those answers before you go”; link the existing checklist in the appropriate profile/caption destination.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain editorial labeling and event-specific checks. Do not suggest all clubs are misleading or that the answers prescribe a medically suitable distance.

episodes.current_title: Two gym days. Build your plan around them.
episodes.current_action: Put the sessions in your calendar and prepare the exercises before you arrive.
episodes.strength: a strong constraint-led topic, concrete calendar visual and permission to plan around reality.
episodes.gap: the highest-value missing answer is which routine can use those two days, not merely putting two ticks in a calendar. “Choose a beginner routine designed for the days” needs an actual resource route.
episodes.proposed_hook: use the existing alternative, “Only two gym days—where do you start?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show available slots becoming two calendar appointments that include travel/setup time and a link to the selected routine. Those extra minutes are scheduling considerations, not fixed prescriptions. End on “Choose a routine for your available days, then reserve the full visit.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain the distinction between adult public-health guidance, program design and maximum gains. Two appointments do not establish training quality or fulfill every activity requirement. Any linked program needs explicit source and scope review.

episodes.current_title: Protein powder is a convenience, not a starting requirement.
episodes.current_action: Start by noticing the protein foods already in your meals.
episodes.strength: useful purchase-friction relief and concrete food categories; no unnecessary supplement sale.
episodes.gap: “notice foods already in your meals” is a weak completion condition. It does not teach me what to do after noticing. The title is longer and less conversational than the saved alternative.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Do you need protein powder to start?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: assemble a sample meal from familiar protein-food options, adapted to budget, preferences and dietary needs. Ask the viewer to identify a protein food in the next meal they are planning. Connect to BP11's meal-planning example instead of asking only whether marketing claims are confusing.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: keep food-first flexibility and no universal intake/dose. “Enough protein,” body-composition goals or individualized amounts would be new questions requiring additional reviewed content; the visible meal must not imply complete nutritional adequacy.

episodes.current_action: Use the log before rewriting the whole routine. A persistent problem deserves a closer review.
episodes.strength: a useful anti-overreaction principle and a specific comparison list: exercise, load, reps, rest and setup.
episodes.gap: I am told to compare like with like but never see an apples-to-oranges comparison. This is an explanatory visual opportunity already supported by the script.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Lifted less today—should you change the whole routine?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show two fictional logs with a changed machine or rest instruction highlighted. End on “Compare the same exercise and conditions before you rewrite the plan.” The log can say “different machine” instead of inventing performance numbers.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain editorial rather than diagnostic framing. Persistent problems deserve review. Do not turn an example into a fixed plateau threshold or recommend ignoring pain, illness or recovery concerns.

episodes.current_title: Tomorrow's lunch starts with what you have.
episodes.current_action: Check your kitchen, then list only what's missing for that meal.
episodes.strength: likely one of the most useful lifestyle episodes on the page: a specific meal, kitchen check and short shopping list. Strong existing action; BPK03 extends it.
episodes.gap: abstract ingredient circles/checklists miss the pleasurable end result. I should see lunch, not just hear that meal planning is sensible.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Tomorrow's lunch—and you don't want another big grocery trip?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show the food already available, the finished illustrative meal and only missing ingredients on a list. End on “Pick tomorrow's lunch, then list only what's missing.” A cooking D scene could fit naturally here.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: meal and list are examples, not nutrition prescriptions. Verify food safety if introducing storage, reheating or batch-cooking instructions; the current “full week” carousel title should not imply that one meal is nutritionally complete or safely stored for a week.

episodes.current_title: Does every set need to end in failure?
episodes.current_action: Follow your routine’s effort guidance and learn the movement with control.
episodes.strength: defines failure and removes the moral framing of effort. The question directly matches common gym language.
episodes.gap: an absolute beginner may not know a rep, set, effort target or RIR yet. A conceptual slider between challenging and failure does not show how a novice follows an instruction.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Does a set only count if you can't finish the last rep?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: begin with a plain-language rep/set example or link a pre-existing glossary. Translate one actual effort instruction from a checked program. End on “Know your routine's stopping rule before the set.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: keep the uncertainty and adult population behind the research synthesis. Do not infer a universal RIR target or suggest beginners estimate proximity to failure precisely. Demonstrating an exertional failure attempt requires more care than an abstract illustration.

episodes.current_title: A better scorecard for month one.
episodes.current_action: Review the month. Pick one thing to improve next time.
episodes.strength: process review avoids a false transformation deadline. Visits, setup skills and recording habits are controllable observations.
episodes.gap: a man who came for aesthetics may hear “look at attendance instead” as avoiding his original goal. Acknowledge the desire and distinguish progress signals from the eventual outcome.
episodes.proposed_hook: “A month in, and the mirror looks the same?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show a three-line check: “Did I attend? Can I set up? Did I record?” Then circle one practical adjustment for the coming week. End on “Choose one thing to improve next week.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain that process metrics are not a body-composition test, and make no appearance deadline. A new timeline, body-measurement method or bulk/cut recommendation needs separate evidence and context.

episodes.current_title: Your workouts have a schedule. Does your sleep?
episodes.current_action: Pick one change that gives sleep a realistic place in your week.
episodes.strength: the current hook is already concise and relevant. It recognizes shift work and caring responsibilities rather than assuming unlimited control.
episodes.gap: “pick one change” gives a tired person another design task. Illustrative clocks do not identify what is crowding sleep out.
episodes.proposed_hook: retain “Your workouts have a schedule. Does your sleep?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: show an ordinary evening calendar, identify one movable task and place a realistic wind-down reminder. Offer this as one option, not the solution for everyone. End on “Choose one feasible schedule change for this week.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: retain BPF03/CDC scope and professional help for ongoing problems. A reminder is an editorial planning tool, not a treatment for insomnia; do not invent a universal bedtime, sleep dose or shift-work cure.

episodes.current_title: Your next activity can start as a tryout.
episodes.current_action: Find one beginner session and check its access requirements before booking.
episodes.strength: expands the brand beyond lifting and allows curiosity without an identity commitment; the closing question is one of the month's most expressive.
episodes.gap: “pick something” and a generic access checklist are broad. The content could be more memorable by showing one ordinary decision while retaining options.
episodes.proposed_hook: “You can try a class without making it your whole personality.”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: compare a fictional beginner session's travel, cost, available instruction and equipment with the viewer's real week. End on “Check one beginner session's practical details.” The existing “What would you try…?” question can stay in the caption or follow-up story.
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: editorial wording and fictional events must be labeled. Do not imply one activity meets every goal, guarantee habit formation, or recommend a paid venue without current verification.

episodes.current_action: Notice what got in the way and make one adjustment you can repeat.
episodes.strength: psychologically kind, practical, and already contains a cause/adjustment loop. Avoiding automatic punishment volume is a useful boundary.
episodes.gap: “one barrier, one adjustment” is shown as an X and a tick; the actual adjustment is missing. This is the clearest opportunity for a short lived scenario.
episodes.proposed_hook: “Work ran late. You missed the gym. Now what?”
episodes.proposed_concrete_action_and_visual: D receives an overtime message; the example calendar checks the routine's missed-day guidance and chooses a realistic next visit. A preparation barrier might become a bag by the door; a schedule barrier might become a different slot. End on “Choose the next session and change one thing that blocked this one.”
episodes.claim_boundary_and_new_evidence_needed: label this a fictional planning example, not individualized programming or a guaranteed adherence method. Do not prescribe replacement volume, reduced volume or recovery timing without checking the actual routine and context.
